title: Collapse node lifecycle states and prune stale capacity planner stitching code
creator: Evelyn Chen
description:
Summary: The capacity planner and GPU fleet node lifecycle codebase contains multiple legacy 'stitching' paths that reconcile legacy lease pools, a fragmented state machine with redundant transitions (PROVISIONING -> STARTING -> READY vs. PROVISIONING -> READY), and duplicated teardown/error-handling logic. This causes surprising edge-cases during scale-down, slower reconciliation loops, and makes reasoning about autoscaler decisions harder.

Goal: Simplify the node lifecycle state machine by collapsing semantically equivalent states, remove the legacy stitching code in the capacity planner that attempts to merge historical lease pools with the new allocator, and centralize error/termination handling into a single reconciler. Aim to reduce tail reconciliation latency, lower code complexity, and reduce incidents related to partial node states during rolling upgrades.

Approach:
- Audit all state transitions and produce a canonical state diagram (PROVISIONING, INITIALIZING, READY, DRAINING, TERMINATING, DECOMMISSIONED). Collapse STARTING/ATTACHING into INITIALIZING where safe.
- Extract the stitching code into a feature-flagged module and write a migration that replays any live legacy leases into the new allocator during a short window; remove the legacy path in a later cutover commit.
- Replace ad-hoc teardown logic with a shared lifecycle handler that emits well-typed events (node.error, node.drained, node.terminated) consumed by the autoscaler.
- Add unit tests for the state transitions and integration tests that run against a local k8s + simulated GPU instance harness.
- Performance validation: run a 24-hour soak with simulated churn (burst scale-up and scale-down) comparing current main vs. refactor branch to measure reconcile latency and tail response percentiles.

Compatibility & Rollout:
- All changes behind two feature flags: "lifecycle-unify" (behavioural changes) and "planner-prune" (stitching removal).
- Canary rollout to dedicated GPU pools in us-west-2 with <5% traffic and telemetry gated.
- Fallback strategy: automatic rollback on increased reconcile failures or any customer-facing error rate spike above 0.5 p.p.

Artifacts: design notes and state diagram in Confluence: https://confluence.internal.redwood/git/GPUPoolLifecycle, design PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood/pull/2197, local test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/test-harness/commit/9a3c2d
acceptance_criteria: Canonical node lifecycle state diagram published and reviewed in Confluence
All legacy stitching code isolated behind 'planner-prune' flag and covered by migration tests
Unit and integration tests added with >=95% coverage for lifecycle code paths
End-to-end soak shows <=10% reduction in reconcile 99th percentile latency or equivalent reduction in reconcile CPU cost
Canary rollout executed with no customer-facing regressions and monitoring dashboards updated
Code reviewed, merged, and release notes + rollback playbook documented
